items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI (`codex-cli 0.155.1`, Windows 11), incl. `codex exec` and multi-agent subagents

### What feature would you like to see?

Please record the model that **served** each turn, next to the model that was **requested**, on the surfaces a
tool can read after the run:

- the rollout file (`~/.codex/sessions/.../rollout-*.jsonl`), e.g. a `served_model` field on the
  `token_usage_record` / `turn_context` for that turn;
- `codex exec --json` (e.g. on `turn.completed`);
- the `SubagentStop` hook payload, as `served_model` alongside the existing `model`.

Codex already has this value. `ResponsesStreamEvent::response_model()` reads the server's `openai-model`
header, and `maybe_warn_on_server_model_mismatch` (`codex-rs/core/src/session/mod.rs`) compares it with the
requested slug. But:

- on a **match** it only writes an INFO log line (`server reported model … (matches requested model)`), which is
  not persisted anywhere a tool can read;
- on a **mismatch** it emits `ModelReroute`, but (at source `4607249e`) always with reason `HighRiskCyberActivity`;
- when the header is **absent**, nothing is recorded, so "matched", "not reported" and "not checked" look the same.

A single persisted field — `served_model: "<id>" | null` (null = server did not report one) — would cover all
three cases.

**Why it matters.** We build a harness that routes subagents to cheaper models by task and must *verify* the
routing (did the cheap tier really run? did an expensive task silently get a cheaper model?). Today every
readable Codex record says the requested model. We probed hooks, rollouts, `exec --json`, app-server v2
(including raw Responses events), OTEL and the local SQLite stores on 0.142.4 → 0.149.1, and re-checked
rollouts on 0.155.1: every model-bearing field echoes the request. An unknown id such as `gpt-9.9-does-not-exist` echoes back unchanged.
On 0.142.5 a dispatch with `model: "codex-auto-review"` (catalog display name GPT-5.6-Luna) was recorded as
`codex-auto-review` on every surface. So a tool cannot tell a requested model from a served one, and it cannot
detect the requested-Astra / served-Luna cases reported in #46632 and #47015.

**Acceptance check.** Spawn a subagent with an explicit `model`. The child rollout and the `SubagentStop`
payload should carry the id from the server's `openai-model` header (or `null` when the server sent none), not
a copy of the requested slug.

### Additional information

- Related: #47354 (asks which field establishes the served model — this request is the persisted form of that
  answer), #46632 and #47015 (requested/served mismatches seen only through wire capture), #32283 (subagent
  model no longer shown in the UI).
- We are not asking for any change to routing, fallback or safety policy — only that the identity Codex
  already receives is written down.
- Useful detail, if easy: keep the `ModelReroute` reason accurate for non-cyber reroutes (capacity, plan
  limits), since it is currently hard-coded.

items.body:
## Summary

On Windows Codex Desktop, a failure in the plugin synchronization path can terminate the local Codex app-server/CLI process. The Desktop UI then reloads and shows the startup splash/logo again, and the currently running task/turn is interrupted.

Disabling plugins with:

```toml
[features]
plugins = false
```

has completely stopped the unexpected Desktop restarts in repeated use.

## Environment

- Platform: Windows x64
- Windows build reported by Codex: `10.0.26100`
- Codex Desktop package: `26.917.9434.0`
- Local app-server version: `0.155.0-alpha.16`
- Local app-server executable observed in logs: `~/.codex/plugins/.plugin-appserver/codex.exe`

## Symptoms

While a Codex task is running:

1. The whole Codex Desktop UI suddenly returns to the initial startup/splash logo.
2. The current task stops.
3. Codex attempts to reinitialize the local app-server.
4. The UI eventually becomes usable again, but the active task has already been interrupted.

This is different from the separate network "Reconnect" behavior. I had this Desktop-restart issue before configuring explicit proxy environment variables. The proxy configuration fixed the repeated Reconnect problem, but did not fix this Desktop restart. Disabling plugins did.

## Relevant log sequence

Immediately before the app-server exits:

```text
Request failed ... read remote plugin details:
failed to send remote plugin catalog request to
https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/ps/plugins/...

chatgpt_pubsub_transport_closed
chatgpt_pubsub_reconnect_scheduled

remote installed plugin bundle sync failed
failed to send remote plugin catalog request to
https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/ps/plugins/installed?limit=200&includeDownloadUrls=true
```

Then:

```text
app_server_connection.closed code=1
app_server_connection.state_changed ... next=error
Codex CLI process exited classifiedAsExpected=false code=1
fatal_error_broadcasted
```

Codex then immediately tries to restart the app-server.

There are also repeated plugin reconciliation warnings later in the same session:

```text
bundled_plugins_reconcile_failed
errorCode=EPERM
errorMessage="EPERM: operation not permitted, unlink
'...\\.codex\\plugins\\.plugin-appserver\\codex.exe'"
```

## Reproduction / isolation

With plugins enabled/default:

1. Launch Codex Desktop on Windows.
2. Start a normal coding task.
3. During use, plugin sync can fail.
4. The local app-server exits with code 1.
5. Desktop reloads to the startup logo and the active task stops.

With:

```toml
[features]
plugins = false
```

the Desktop has remained stable and the unexpected reload/restart has stopped.

## Expected behavior

A plugin catalog/synchronization/network failure should be isolated from the core app-server lifecycle. It should fail gracefully, retry, or temporarily disable the affected plugin functionality without terminating the Codex app-server or interrupting the user's active coding task.

The `EPERM` file-lock failure while reconciling `.plugin-appserver/codex.exe` may also be relevant to the Windows-specific failure path.

## Additional note

Please do not treat the proxy environment configuration as the cause of this crash. The Desktop restart behavior existed beforehand. Explicit proxy configuration only resolved a separate repeated-Reconnect issue; `plugins = false` is what eliminated the Desktop restart.

items.title: ChatGPT Pro 20x: every model I pick is silently served by gpt-5.6-luna

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: model-behavior
labels.description: Issues related to behaviors exhibited by the model

items.body:
I'm on ChatGPT Pro 20x. For a while now Codex has felt way dumber than it should, no matter which model I pick. So I stopped guessing and measured it.

**Short version: on my account, the model picker is fake.** gpt-5.6-sol, gpt-6-luna, gpt-6-sol, gpt-6-astra all answer exactly like gpt-5.6-luna. I'm getting one model under five different names.

## How I tested

I used one-token fingerprinting, the same approach the model-substitution papers use. You ask tiny "just pick one" questions (random number, color, city, animal, coin flip, etc.), sample each one a bunch of times, and compare the answer distributions. Different models have different favorites, so the distribution works as a fingerprint.

- 5 models × 16 prompts (8 EN / 8 ZH) × 25 samples = 2,000 requests
- Every request used the same instructions, `temperature=1.0`, and `reasoning.effort=low`
- I compared the distributions with Jensen-Shannon divergence and a 1,000-round permutation test, Bonferroni-corrected (α = 0.005)

## Results

**None of the 10 model pairs is statistically distinguishable.** The median JSD is 0.046, which is just sampling noise. These are supposed to be five different models across two generations. They shouldn't be giving the same answers.

"Give me a random number between 1 and 100", 25 tries each:

| Model I picked | Answers |
|---|---|
| gpt-5.6-luna | 47×13, 73×12 |
| gpt-5.6-sol | 73×13, 47×12 |
| gpt-6-luna | 73×13, 47×9, 37×2, 57×1 |
| gpt-6-sol | 47×12, 73×9, 57×2, 37×2 |
| gpt-6-astra | 47×13, 73×9, 37×2, 57×1 |

For "Name a random color", all five say teal or cerulean almost every time. For "Name a random city", all five pick Reykjavik, Kyoto or Lisbon. The other prompts show the same pattern.

## This isn't OK

I'm paying for Pro 20x. When I pick gpt-6-astra, I get gpt-5.6-luna. There's been no notice, no warning and no explanation. If my account is limited for some reason, tell me. Quietly swapping in an older model while the picker keeps showing the one I chose is a bait-and-switch.

## What I want

1. A straight answer: is my account being rerouted, and why?
2. If a request is served by a different model, show that. Don't let the picker list models I'm not actually getting.
3. Fix it, or give me a way to appeal.

I can share the raw samples and the script if anyone on the team wants to check.

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

codex-cli 0.156.1

### What subscription do you have?

Unknown / not relevant to terminal rendering

### Which model were you using?

_No response_

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 25.5.0 arm64 arm

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

iTerm2 3.6.4 (no multiplexer)

### Codex doctor report

```json
Ran `codex doctor --json`; full report omitted because it contains local filesystem paths and account-specific configuration.
```

### What issue are you seeing?

When an otherwise idle Codex TUI session loses focus in iTerm2, its tab shows iTerm2's blue unread-output dot within a few seconds, although no task is running and no new response appears. The tab sometimes briefly shows 'Loading' before the dot; I have not established where that text originates.

A controlled PTY capture shows that focus loss itself makes idle Codex write terminal control sequences. After startup, there were 0 output bytes during a 3-second idle period. Sending the focus-out sequence `ESC [ O` then yielded 39 bytes immediately:

```text
\x1b[?2026h\x1b[m\x1b[m\x1b[0m\x1b[11;3H\x1b[?25h\x1b[?2026l
```

This is a synchronized-update wrapper, ANSI resets and cursor control, with no new visible content or terminal-title OSC sequence. iTerm2 treats the background output as unread output and marks the tab with a blue dot.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Open an iTerm2 tab and run `codex`. Wait until the TUI is idle at the input prompt.
2. Switch to another iTerm2 tab.
3. Within seconds, observe the background Codex tab's blue unread-output dot.

In a PTY with `TERM=xterm-256color` and `TERM_PROGRAM=iTerm.app`, send `ESC [ O` to the idle Codex process to reproduce the terminal output without a real tab switch.

### What is the expected behavior?

An idle Codex TUI should not emit terminal output solely because it lost focus. iTerm2 should only show unread output when Codex has actually produced new content.

### Additional information

Disabling `Session → Terminal State → Focus Reporting` in the affected iTerm2 tab stops the symptom, but must be done per tab. iTerm2 also offers `Settings → Advanced → Apps may turn on Focus Reporting = No` as a broader workaround; that disables focus reporting for all terminal apps.

Changing `tui.animations` and using a static `tui.terminal_title` did not resolve the observed symptom, and those local settings have been reverted. The PTY capture contains no title OSC sequence, so this seems distinct from #16332.

items.title: [Windows] UNKNOWN/-4094 copy fallback causes ~10x runtime relocation slowdown and blocks Electron main thread

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.917.9434.0

### What subscription do you have?

Plus

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64

### What issue are you seeing?

This may share the same overall first-launch runtime-materialization path as #45179 and #46338, but this report isolates a more specific implementation-level performance defect in the **current successful `UNKNOWN/-4094` fallback path**.

Older reports such as #34764 / #42501 describe `copyfile UNKNOWN / errno -4094` causing runtime relocation to fail. On `26.917.9434.0`, relocation eventually succeeds because the app now falls back to synchronous byte-stream copying - but on this machine that fallback itself causes a severe performance regression.

### Observed startup behavior

First launch after the update:

- host startup critical path: ~225.98 s
- `cua_node` materialization occupies roughly ~212 s
- the main window is only revealed after materialization is effectively complete

A startup log line shows:

```
Failed to load shell env ... timeoutMs=5000 durationMs=219869 status=timed_out
```

Second launch of the same version:

- host startup critical path: ~4.63 s
- window ready-to-show in <1 s
- the same shell-env timeout completes in ~5.08 s

This suggests PowerShell is not taking ~220 s. The Electron main event loop appears to be blocked during first-launch runtime relocation, so the 5 s timer itself cannot run on time.

### Experiment 1: identify what is created during the slow launch

For the `cua_node` runtime:

- 2,283 files
- ~239 MB
- source: packaged `app\resources\cua_node`
- destination: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\runtimes\cua_node\<hash>`

Across the full first-launch relocation window, about 2,288 files / ~640.3 MB are created under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex`. The timestamps line up closely with the period in which the UI is unavailable.

### Experiment 2: rule out raw source-read performance

Reading the complete 2,283-file tree without writing:

```
WindowsApps source tree:
  2,283 files / 239 MB
  1.119 s
  ~213.5 MB/s

Already-materialized local tree:
  2,283 files / 239 MB
  0.543 s
  ~440.2 MB/s
```

Raw packaged-runtime reads are therefore fast enough that source-read throughput does not explain a multi-minute stall.

### Experiment 3: controlled normal tree copy

Using a straightforward byte-stream tree copy outside the ChatGPT code path:

```
WindowsApps source -> temp:
  13.201 s
  172.9 files/s
  ~18.1 MB/s

Local materialized source -> temp:
  12.717 s
  179.5 files/s
  ~18.8 MB/s
```

The results are very close, so the secondary AppX volume / cross-volume layout alone does not explain the delay.

### Experiment 4: inspect the current relocation implementation

The packaged `app.asar` relocation helper effectively does this per file:

```js
try {
  fs.copyFileSync(src, dst)
} catch (e) {
  // handles errno 6000 or UNKNOWN/-4094
  fs.writeFileSync(dst, fs.readFileSync(src))
}
```

The surrounding traversal/validation path also uses synchronous filesystem APIs such as `readdirSync`, `copyFileSync`, `readFileSync`, `writeFileSync`, `mkdirSync`, and `renameSync`.

### Experiment 5: reproduce the current fallback strategy

I reproduced the same strategy in a minimal Node.js test:

1. recursively enumerate the packaged `cua_node` tree;
2. call `fs.copyFileSync(src, dst)` for every file;
3. on `UNKNOWN/-4094`, fall back to `fs.readFileSync(src)` + `fs.writeFileSync(dst)`;
4. count direct-copy successes and fallback hits;
5. delete the temporary output after the benchmark.

Result:

```
files:       2283
size:        239 MB
elapsed:     127.98 s
files/sec:   17.8
throughput:  ~1.9 MB/s

copyFileSync direct success: 0
fallback path:              2283
other errors:               0
```

Every one of the 2,283 files first failed with:

```
code = UNKNOWN
errno = -4094
syscall = copyfile
```

before taking the synchronous fallback.

Key comparison:

```
normal byte-stream copy:   ~13.2 s
current fallback strategy: ~128.0 s
actual first launch:       ~226.0 s
```

So reproducing the current fallback strategy is already about 10x slower than a straightforward copy on the same machine, before accounting for the rest of Electron startup work.

### Interpretation

The current fallback appears to solve the older functional failure (runtime relocation eventually succeeds), but it can convert that failure into a multi-minute startup stall:

```
new runtime hash missing
  -> relocation starts
  -> copyFileSync fails for every packaged file with UNKNOWN/-4094
  -> every file pays exception + fallback cost
  -> synchronous readFileSync/writeFileSync for thousands of files
  -> Electron main process is blocked
  -> timers/window startup are delayed
  -> relocation finishes
  -> subsequent launches are fast because the runtime hash now exists
```

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Install/update Codex App from Microsoft Store/MSIX to a build whose runtime hash has not yet been materialized locally.
2. Launch the app for the first time after the update.
3. Observe that the usable window is delayed for minutes while files are created under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\runtimes` and `bin`.
4. Close the app after it becomes usable.
5. Launch the same version again; startup returns to a few seconds.
6. To reproduce the implementation-level slowdown independently, run the same per-file strategy against the packaged `cua_node` tree: try `fs.copyFileSync`, catch `UNKNOWN/-4094`, then use `fs.readFileSync` + `fs.writeFileSync`. On this machine all 2,283 files hit the fallback and the test takes ~127.98 s, versus ~13.2 s for a straightforward byte-stream copy of the same tree.

### What is the expected behavior?

Runtime materialization after an update should not block the Electron main thread for minutes. If packaged files consistently require an alternate copy path, the app should avoid thousands of predictable failed `copyFileSync` attempts and perform the relocation without delaying window creation, IPC, and timers. A first launch should remain responsive and complete in roughly the same order of magnitude as a normal copy of the bundled runtime.

### Additional information

Related reports: #45179, #46338, #34764, #42501.

This issue intentionally focuses on the **performance regression in the fallback that now succeeds**, rather than the older hard relocation failure.

Potential implementation directions suggested by the measurements:

- detect the `UNKNOWN/-4094` source condition once and switch the whole tree to the alternate copy path instead of throwing/catching per file;
- use a Windows-native copy path with the appropriate packaged/protected-file semantics instead of generic Node `copyFileSync` followed by fallback;
- move runtime materialization to a worker/child process so it cannot block the Electron main event loop;
- where possible, materialize during update/install staging rather than on the first user-visible launch.

Windows Defender real-time protection was disabled during these measurements, which makes Defender an unlikely explanation for the measured ~10x difference between the two copy strategies.

I can provide exact startup-log excerpts and the minimal Node.js reproduction script if useful.

items.title: [Windows] End-to-end workaround: rename_staging EPERM -> sandbox helper missing -> code-mode host missing with CODEX_CLI_PATH

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
## Summary

This is a consolidated Windows field report and workaround for a chain of Codex Desktop failures I hit on 2026-09-24.

Related reports:
- #45593 — `rename_staging` / `EPERM` during bundled runtime relocation
- #45858 — startup failure after Store update for CLI + Node runtime
- #41088 — local execution fails because code-mode host cannot start
- #38975 — missing / incorrectly packaged code-mode host
- #46155 — stale per-user backend when `CODEX_CLI_PATH` survives an app update

The important part is that the first workaround can expose a second and third failure if only `codex.exe` is copied. The working workaround required a **matching set of companion binaries**, with hash checks, and avoiding mixing binaries from different app/runtime builds.

---

## Environment

- Windows 11 x64
- PowerShell 5.1.26100.9444
- Microsoft Store / MSIX package: `OpenAI.Codex`
- Initial affected app package: `26.917.8451.0`
- Later package during troubleshooting: `26.917.9434.0`
- Working CLI/runtime build used by the workaround: `codex-cli 0.155.0-alpha.16.3`

Paths below are sanitized to use `%USERPROFILE%`.

---

## Failure 1 — Desktop app cannot start

The app failed immediately with:

```text
ChatGPT failed to start.
Unable to locate the Codex CLI binary or required runtime components.
Check the installation or explicit runtime overrides.
```

A clean uninstall/reinstall, removal of local runtime data, reboot, and reinstall did **not** fix it.

The packaged `codex.exe` was present under the MSIX `app\resources` directory, so the binary was not actually missing.

The desktop logs showed the real failure:

```text
bundled_executable_relocation_failed
errorCode=EPERM
operation=rename_staging
syscall=rename
```

This happened for both:
- `codex.exe`
- `cua_node` runtime components such as `node.exe` / `node_repl.exe`

Example pattern:

```text
%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\bin\.staging-<hash>-XXXX
    -> %LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\bin\<hash>
```

The rename failed with Windows `EPERM`.

### Why this did not look like a static ACL problem

- The user had FullControl on the target directories.
- A manually created staging directory in the same location could be renamed successfully.
- The packaged `codex.exe` could be copied out and run successfully.
- The final target directory did not already exist.
- Therefore the generic "Unable to locate Codex CLI" error was downstream of the runtime deployment failure.

This matches the behavior discussed in #45593 / #45858.

---

## Workaround stage 1 — stable external CLI path

I copied the bundled/managed `codex.exe` to a stable directory that the desktop app would not clean:

```text
%USERPROFILE%\CodexCLI\codex.exe
```

Then set:

```text
CODEX_CLI_PATH=%USERPROFILE%\CodexCLI\codex.exe
```

After reboot, the desktop app could start.

However, this exposed the next issue.

---

## Failure 2 — sandbox helper missing

Windows then showed:

```text
Windows cannot find file 'codex-windows-sandbox-setup.exe'
```

The custom `CodexCLI` directory initially contained only `codex.exe`.

The package did contain the required helper binaries, so I copied the matching helpers next to the overridden CLI:

```text
%USERPROFILE%\CodexCLI\
  codex.exe
  codex-windows-sandbox-setup.exe
  codex-command-runner.exe
```

After that, normal desktop startup and Windows sandbox setup succeeded.

---

## Failure 3 — Work / local execution still broken

The desktop UI now worked, but Work/local execution failed before PowerShell commands were started:

```text
failed to spawn code-mode host
%USERPROFILE%\CodexCLI\codex-code-mode-host.exe:
The system cannot find the file specified. (os error 2)
```

This made the actual problem obvious:

When `CODEX_CLI_PATH` points to a custom `codex.exe`, the code-mode host is resolved as a sibling of that executable.

The custom directory did not contain:

```text
codex-code-mode-host.exe
```

But the OpenAI-managed runtime **did** contain it:

```text
%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\bin\<runtime-hash>\codex-code-mode-host.exe
```

---

## Critical version/hash check before copying the host

During troubleshooting, the Store app updated from `26.917.8451.0` to `26.917.9434.0`.

The newer MSIX `codex.exe` and `codex-code-mode-host.exe` were **not** the same build as the already-working overridden runtime.

So I did **not** copy the host blindly from the newest MSIX package.

Instead I compared SHA256 hashes.

The external override CLI:

```text
%USERPROFILE%\CodexCLI\codex.exe
SHA256:
A19F8F6C3C9DD5B71B6B1E3EB1EC55D75AAFB2FDFB686D9E1F7A5F47DB07D0D2
```

The OpenAI-managed runtime CLI:

```text
%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\bin\80f78947ad880e6e\codex.exe
SHA256:
A19F8F6C3C9DD5B71B6B1E3EB1EC55D75AAFB2FDFB686D9E1F7A5F47DB07D0D2
```

They were identical.

The matching host in that same managed runtime was:

```text
%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\bin\80f78947ad880e6e\codex-code-mode-host.exe
SHA256:
75B016E16EDF3F3A1253EC922EB6B129C5355353399FD9107FA6181D8DFD41C7
```

By contrast, the newer `26.917.9434.0` MSIX binaries had different hashes/sizes.

This is important: **do not mix a host from a newer package with an older overridden CLI just because the filenames match.**

---

## Workaround stage 2 — copy the matching code-mode host

After verifying the CLI hashes matched, I copied the host from the **same managed runtime build**:

```powershell
$src = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\OpenAI\Codex\bin\80f78947ad880e6e\codex-code-mode-host.exe"
$dst = "$env:USERPROFILE\CodexCLI\codex-code-mode-host.exe"

Copy-Item $src $dst -Force
```

Then verified the copied file hash matched the source.

Final working custom directory:

```text
%USERPROFILE%\CodexCLI\
  codex.exe
  codex-code-mode-host.exe
  codex-command-runner.exe
  codex-windows-sandbox-setup.exe
```

After fully exiting and reopening the desktop app:

- Desktop startup succeeded
- Sandbox initialization succeeded
- Work/local execution succeeded
- A read-only command could list the user directory normally

So the end-to-end workaround was successful.

---

## Data-safety warning: back up `.codex` before cleanup/reset

During troubleshooting, I learned that deleting/resetting `%USERPROFILE%\.codex` can remove or detach local project/task state.

Before any cleanup or binary workaround, I now recommend copying at least:

```text
%USERPROFILE%\.codex
%USERPROFILE%\CodexCLI
```

In particular, preserve:

```text
sessions
archived_sessions
sqlite
*.sqlite
*-wal
*-shm
.codex-global-state.json
session_index.jsonl
```

SQLite WAL/SHM files should be backed up together with their database files.

Do not assume an empty Projects sidebar means all session/task data is gone.

---

## Minimal diagnostic commands

### 1. Check package + runtime

```powershell
$pkg = Get-AppxPackage OpenAI.Codex
$pkg | Select-Object Name,Version,PackageFullName,InstallLocation

Get-ChildItem $pkg.InstallLocation -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
Where-Object { $_.Name -match '^codex.*\.exe$' } |
Select-Object Name,FullName,Length
```

### 2. Check override

```powershell
[PSCustomObject]@{
  Process = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("CODEX_CLI_PATH","Process")
  User    = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("CODEX_CLI_PATH","User")
  Machine = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("CODEX_CLI_PATH","Machine")
}
```

### 3. Check whether host exists beside overridden CLI

```powershell
$cli = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("CODEX_CLI_PATH","User")
$dir = Split-Path $cli

Get-ChildItem $dir -Force |
Select-Object Name,Length,FullName
```

### 4. Verify hashes before mixing binaries

```powershell
Get-FileHash <path-to-codex.exe> -Algorithm SHA256
Get-FileHash <path-to-codex-code-mode-host.exe> -Algorithm SHA256
```

---

## Suggested product fixes

1. Make Windows `rename_staging` deployment tolerant of transient `EPERM` / sharing conflicts.
2. Serialize runtime relocation for a given hash and retry with backoff.
3. Surface the actual failed deployment operation instead of only saying the CLI is "missing".
4. If `CODEX_CLI_PATH` is set, validate that required sibling binaries exist:
   - `codex-code-mode-host.exe`
   - sandbox setup/runner helpers
5. On app/MSIX update, detect a stale overridden CLI/runtime and warn before launching.
6. Do not silently combine binaries from different runtime builds.
7. Provide a supported command/action to rebuild the local runtime cache without deleting user session/task data.
8. Document which files are user data vs disposable runtime cache so troubleshooting does not accidentally destroy project/task history.

---

## Result

The app is now working normally again, including Work/local execution.

The key lesson was that the initial startup failure, sandbox helper failure, and code-mode-host failure were all connected through the Windows runtime deployment path and the `CODEX_CLI_PATH` workaround.

A partial workaround containing only `codex.exe` is not enough; the matching companion binaries must be available as well, and their build compatibility should be verified before copying.

The 32 KiB per-result cap and 128 KiB aggregate budget discard tool metadata even when the outgoing request has room to retain it.

- Record bytes removed by metadata budgets in `codex.tool_metadata.shed_bytes`, tagged by stage.

`codex-cli 0.156.1` (Windows x64, standalone installation). The immediately previous official Windows release, `0.155.0`, works with the same MCP server and configuration.

### What subscription do you have?

Not specified. The failure occurs during MCP OAuth metadata discovery, before any model request.

### Which model were you using?

Not applicable; this is reproducible with `codex mcp login`.

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64 (Windows 11 Professional), native Windows CLI.

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

Windows Terminal, PowerShell.

### Codex doctor report

`codex doctor --json` reports the standalone installation and MCP configuration as locally consistent, with no proxy environment variables configured. The full report is omitted because it contains local filesystem paths and account-state details.

### What issue are you seeing?

On native Windows, `codex mcp login <server>` fails before opening the OAuth authorization page:

```text
Error: Metadata error: OAuth metadata discovery failed for https://<mcp-host>/mcp
  Caused by: HTTP request failed: error decoding response body
```

The MCP server is configured as Streamable HTTP. Its protected-resource metadata endpoint and the Entra OIDC discovery endpoint both return HTTP 200 with valid JSON when fetched using `curl.exe`. The same failure occurs when invoking `codex mcp login` directly, so it is not caused by the PowerShell installer wrapper. The saved MCP URL and requested scope are correct, and no proxy is configured.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. On native Windows x64, install Codex CLI 0.156.1 and configure a Streamable HTTP MCP server at `https://<mcp-host>/mcp` that responds to unauthenticated requests with HTTP 401 and a valid `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://<mcp-host>/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp"` challenge.
2. Confirm that the advertised protected-resource metadata URL returns a valid JSON document pointing to a valid OAuth/OIDC authorization server metadata document.
3. Run `codex mcp login <server>`.
4. Observe the metadata discovery error above.

### What feature would you like to see?
We would like Codex to permit subagent roles (configured in `.codex/agents/<role>.toml`, e.g., `worker.toml`, `explorer.toml`, or custom roles) to specify and use alternative or local OpenAI-compatible model providers (such as local proxies/routers, Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM), even when the main coordinator/parent thread is authenticated via a ChatGPT subscription account (`auth_provider = "chatgpt"`).

Currently, when the ChatGPT parent agent attempts to delegate tasks to a subagent role that declares a custom provider/model, the tool dispatcher blocks the spawn:
```text
ERROR codex_core::tools::router: error=The selected agent uses a non-OpenAI model provider; retry with the corresponding `external_agents` collaboration tool.
```

### Steps to Reproduce
1. Configure a subagent role in `~/.codex/agents/worker.toml`:
   ```toml
   model = "custom-subagent-model"
   provider = "my-local-gateway"
   ```
2. In Codex (CLI, VS Code, or Desktop), start a session authenticated with ChatGPT (`chatgpt.com` auth mode, model `gpt-5.5` or `gpt-6-luna`).
3. Issue a prompt requiring parallel subagent delegation:
   *"Please delegate to a worker subagent to inspect package.json and summarize dependencies."*
4. The parent model attempts to invoke the delegation tool, but `codex_core::tools::router` intercepts the call and fails with:
   `error=The selected agent uses a non-OpenAI model provider; retry with the corresponding 'external_agents' collaboration tool.`

### Expected Behavior
Codex should permit the spawned subagent thread to initialize with the provider and endpoint configured in its role definition file (`.codex/agents/<role>.toml`), allowing hybrid multi-agent delegation without requiring the parent coordinator to switch away from its primary ChatGPT subscription session.

### Value & Use Case
1. **Quota & Efficiency Optimization**: Multi-agent delegation often handles repetitive, read-heavy, or exploratory subtasks (e.g. searching large file trees, summarizing lockfiles, running localized linters). Allowing subagents to use local or developer-routed models preserves primary ChatGPT reasoning quota for the coordinator.
2. **Hybrid Multi-Agent Architectures**: Developers can leverage state-of-the-art OpenAI models for high-level reasoning and planning, while delegating high-volume bounded subtasks to self-hosted or domain-specialized models.

### Proposed Solutions
- Allow `codex-rs/core/src/tools/router.rs` to route subagent creation requests to the client instance associated with the role's declared provider.
- Alternatively, provide an explicit configuration opt-in in `config.toml`:
  ```toml
  [multi_agent]
  allow_cross_provider_subagents = true
  ```

- Platform: macOS

### What issue are you seeing?

A repository-local Skill can remain bound to the original checkout after the same task begins operating in a fresh linked Git worktree for the same repository.

In the observed case:

- The original checkout contained an older `.agents/skills/example-delivery/SKILL.md`.
- That older Skill required a repository entrypoint that existed in the older revision.
- The task created a dedicated worktree from the latest main revision and continued the implementation there.
- In the worktree, the same repo-local Skill had already been updated and the old entrypoint had intentionally been removed.
- Codex nevertheless continued following the Skill content loaded from the original checkout.
- It attempted the retired procedure, failed because the entrypoint no longer existed in the active worktree, and blocked the task.
- Codex later noticed that the worktree contained a newer version of the Skill, but treated switching to it as something requiring user approval.

The repository state in the worktree was internally consistent. The inconsistency was between the checkout used for execution and the checkout used as the authority for repo-local Skill instructions.

This means a stale repo-local Skill from one checkout can govern commands, file reads, and workflow decisions executed against another checkout of the same repository.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

A minimal synthetic reproduction should be possible with two revisions of the same repository:

1. In commit A, add `.agents/skills/example-delivery/SKILL.md` that instructs the agent to run `node tools/old-entrypoint.mjs`. Include that entrypoint in commit A.
2. In commit B on the repository's current main branch, update the same Skill so it no longer uses that entrypoint, and delete `tools/old-entrypoint.mjs`.
3. Keep a local checkout at commit A while main is at commit B.
4. Start a Codex App task from the checkout at A and invoke the repo-local Skill.
5. From the same task, create or transition into a linked Git worktree at commit B and continue the task from that worktree.
6. Confirm that file operations and implementation work are now targeting the worktree at B.
7. Observe that Codex still follows the Skill instructions loaded from the original checkout at A.
8. The task attempts `tools/old-entrypoint.mjs` and fails or blocks, even though the active worktree contains a newer valid `.agents/skills/example-delivery/SKILL.md`.

The key condition is that the logical repository Skill exists at the same repository-relative path in both checkouts, but its contents changed between revisions.

### What is the expected behavior?

When the effective task workspace moves from one checkout to another worktree of the same Git repository, repo-local Skill authority should move with it.

Before continuing execution in the new worktree, Codex should re-resolve repo-local Skill roots from that worktree and ensure the model-visible Skill instructions match the active checkout.

At minimum, Codex should never silently use `<original-checkout>/.agents/skills/.../SKILL.md` as the workflow authority while executing against `<worktree>/.agents/skills/.../SKILL.md` when those files differ.

If hot rebinding within an existing task is intentionally unsupported, Codex should detect the mismatch and require an explicit supported handoff or a new task before executing further. It should not continue with stale Skill instructions.

### Additional information

This appears related to, but distinct from:

- #34352, where "Continue in worktree" updates some worktree metadata while the runtime remains attached to the original checkout.
- #35152, where repository Skill enablement is keyed by absolute path and therefore changes identity across worktrees.
- #16607, where resumed threads keep a stale model-visible Skill inventory.

The distinguishing symptom here is stale **Skill content and authority**: the task is operating against one checkout while workflow instructions from another checkout continue to govern execution.

A robust invariant would be that a repo-local Skill is identified by the logical Git project plus its repository-relative Skill path, while the loaded content is resolved from the task's current effective workspace revision.

Useful regression coverage would include a linked-worktree case where the same repo-local Skill changes between two commits and an entrypoint required by the older Skill is deleted in the newer revision. After the task moves to the newer worktree, only the newer Skill must be visible and executable.

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

`codex-cli 0.155.0-alpha.16.3` (bundled with Codex Desktop `OpenAI.Codex 26.917.8451.0`), reproduced deterministically.
Also observed in the field with `codex-cli 0.145.0-alpha.4` (npm). The relevant code is unchanged on `main` at [`7dae8c5`](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/7dae8c53d97e61cd774e4d6bcca5243c29ca615c).

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200, Git for Windows. Marketplace: `https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad.git` (~300 MB full clone).

### What issue are you seeing?

This is a root-cause report for the `.staging` leak tracked in #39421 / #45943, with a deterministic repro.

**A graceful `codex app-server` shutdown (exit code 0) orphans an in-flight marketplace `git clone`.** The startup marketplace auto-upgrade runs on a detached `std::thread`, and the `git` child it spawns is only ever killed on the 30 s timeout path. If the process exits first, neither `child.kill()` nor `TempDir::drop` runs: git keeps going, finishes a full clone into `.staging/marketplace-upgrade-*`, and nothing is logged.

Any client that uses `codex app-server` for short tasks triggers this on every launch. On my machine that is a third-party usage monitor (Metrik), which spawns a fresh `codex app-server` every 1–4 minutes. OpenAI's own Claude Code plugin works the same way: [`codex-plugin-cc` `app-server.mjs#L190`](https://github.com/openai/codex-plugin-cc/blob/db52e28f4d9ded852ab3942cea316258ae4ef346/plugins/codex/scripts/lib/app-server.mjs#L190) spawns `codex app-server` per task.

**This correction matters for the existing threads:** on this machine the 30 s timeout path does **not** leak. All 11 logged `git clone marketplace source timed out after 30s` failures had their staging dir removed. The leaked dirs are the ones that never produced a log line.

### Steps to reproduce

Precondition: a configured git marketplace whose remote `HEAD` differs from the installed revision. This happens whenever the upstream repo gets a new commit, and it stays true because short-lived processes never finish the upgrade (see below).

1. Start `codex app-server` with piped stdio and send `initialize`, as an integration client would.
2. Wait until `git clone` starts. That took 5.3 s here: ls-remote for each marketplace, then the clone.
3. Close stdin, i.e. the client disconnects.

Observed on `0.155.0-alpha.16.3`:

```
11:07:41.540  app-server started pid=16200
11:07:43.915  git child: git ls-remote https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad.git HEAD
11:07:46.875  git child: git clone https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad.git ...\.staging\marketplace-upgrade-fRNUA3
11:07:49.347  closing app-server stdin (graceful client disconnect)
11:07:49.370  app-server exited, code=0
t+120 s       git children still alive: 3 [git clone, git remote-https, git-remote-https]
              staging dir still present
```

The installed marketplace was not touched. It is still at its old revision, so the next launch will clone again.

### Root cause in code (permalinks at `7dae8c5`)

1. [`core-plugins/src/manager.rs#L2796-L2803`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/7dae8c53d97e61cd774e4d6bcca5243c29ca615c/codex-rs/core-plugins/src/manager.rs#L2796-L2803): every process with plugins enabled spawns a **detached** `std::thread` named `plugins-marketplace-auto-upgrade` at startup. The `in_flight` guard is process-local, so every new process starts its own attempt.
2. [`core-plugins/src/marketplace_upgrade.rs#L241-L282`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/7dae8c53d97e61cd774e4d6bcca5243c29ca615c/codex-rs/core-plugins/src/marketplace_upgrade.rs#L241-L282): `git ls-remote` runs, then a `TempDir` is created under `.staging`, then `clone_git_source` runs synchronously on that thread.
3. [`core-plugins/src/marketplace_upgrade/git.rs#L183-L224`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/7dae8c53d97e61cd774e4d6bcca5243c29ca615c/codex-rs/core-plugins/src/marketplace_upgrade/git.rs#L183-L224): `std::process::Child` is polled with `try_wait()` plus `sleep(100ms)`, and `child.kill()` exists only in the timeout branch. When the process exits, the detached thread is torn down without unwinding. `std::process::Child` has no kill-on-drop, and on Windows children are not killed with their parent unless a job object is used. So the clone runs to completion into an unowned directory.

This also explains why most orphans reported in #39421 / #45943 are **complete** clones rather than partial ones.

### Field evidence (one machine, 2026-09-18 → 2026-09-24)

- **95 orphaned `marketplace-upgrade-*` dirs, 16.2 GB.** 56 are complete clones and 39 are stubs. **None of them appears in `logs_2.sqlite`.**
- **For 92 of 95, the codex process that was logging when the dir was created stopped logging ≤ 5 s later.** Over the 10-day log window, **1,197 codex processes lived under 1 minute**, and their dominant log targets are `codex_app_server*`.
- **For the complete orphans, git wrote `.git/logs/HEAD` 17 s to 30 min after the dir was created (median 39 s)**, i.e. after the parent had already exited.
- **I caught one live.** Process chain: `metrik.exe → cmd /C codex.cmd app-server → node codex.js app-server → codex.exe app-server (pid 35848)`. 2.2 s later, `git ls-remote https://github.com/sendbird/codex-marketplace.git HEAD` was still running and its grandparent `35848` was gone.
- **The leak is self-perpetuating.** The installed revision has been stuck at `4ebbd2cc` since `last_updated = 2026-09-19T01:58:51Z`. Upstream moved to `4eaf7459` around 2026-09-22, and there are **32 complete clones of `4eaf7459`, none of them activated**. Every new short-lived process sees remote ≠ installed and clones again. The previous upstream commit went the same way: 23 complete clones of `4ebbd2cc` piled up before one attempt finally activated it.

### Expected behavior

- Starting and stopping `codex app-server` should never leave `git` processes or `.staging` directories behind.
- A client that only wants to read something should not trigger a ~300 MB clone.

### Suggested fixes

1. **Tie git's lifetime to the process.** On Windows, put the git child in a Job Object with `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE`. On Unix, use a process group that is killed on shutdown. Also make the upgrade cancellable, so app-server shutdown kills the child and drops the `TempDir` deterministically.
2. **Don't run the startup auto-upgrade in every app-server process.** For example, run it only in long-lived hosts (Desktop/TUI), defer it until a client actually calls a plugin API, or gate it with a cross-process lock plus a persisted last-attempt timestamp. The last option also addresses #36093.
3. **Sweep stale `.staging/marketplace-upgrade-*` at startup** (older than N minutes), mirroring `remove_stale_curated_repo_temp_dirs`. The same sweep can cover the `git-*` temp dirs in `.tmp/` reported in #39421.

### Additional information

**A note on the `ref`-pinning workaround from #39421.** From reading [`activation.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/7dae8c53d97e61cd774e4d6bcca5243c29ca615c/codex-rs/core-plugins/src/marketplace_upgrade/activation.rs#L68-L74), `installed_marketplace_metadata_matches` compares `ref_name` too, and an existing install has `"ref_name": null`. So adding `ref = "<sha>"` to `config.toml` forces one reinstall clone before the shortcut kicks in. If the only processes running are short-lived ones, that reinstall leaks the same way. I haven't tested this; it is inferred from the code.

Related: #39421, #45943, #36093.

items.title: Replayed reasoning items send "content": null, which the Responses API schema does not permit

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: custom-model
labels.description: Issues related to custom model providers (including local models)

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

codex-cli 0.154.0, where I reproduced it. The code involved has not changed since then: the `content` attribute and `should_serialize_reasoning_content` are identical at `rust-v0.154.0`, `rust-v0.156.1`, and `main` at `7dae8c53`.

### What subscription do you have?

Not relevant here. The requests go to a custom `model_providers` entry that uses that provider's API key.

### Which model were you using?

`grok-4.6` on xAI, configured with `wire_api = "responses"` and `-c model_reasoning_effort=high`.

### What platform is your computer?

Linux 6.6.114.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2 x86_64 x86_64

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

Not relevant. I reproduced it with non-interactive `codex exec`.

### Codex doctor report

Not included. The defect is in request-body serialization and does not depend on install, config, or auth state. I can attach it if it helps.

### What issue are you seeing?

**When Codex replays a reasoning item on the next turn, it serializes an absent `content` as `"content": null`. OpenAI's published Responses schema has no null branch for that field.** Providers that validate request bodies against the schema reject the request, which breaks every multi-turn task that replays reasoning. OpenAI's own endpoint accepts the null, so this does not show up with first-party models.

This has the same root cause as #11834. That issue was closed as "sounds like a bug in OpenRouter", which is a fair reading if the provider is stricter than the spec. The spec evidence below points the other way: the value is not permitted, so the strict provider is the conformant one.

**The predicate is inverted for `None`.** The attribute is at [`models.rs` L1052](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/b412ff32c417f855c2b2d1581b77058eed87c84b/codex-rs/protocol/src/models.rs#L1052) and the function at [L1623-L1630](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/b412ff32c417f855c2b2d1581b77058eed87c84b/codex-rs/protocol/src/models.rs#L1623-L1630) (`rust-v0.156.1`):

```rust
    Reasoning {
        ...
        #[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "should_serialize_reasoning_content")]
        #[ts(optional)]
        content: Option<Vec<ReasoningItemContent>>,
        encrypted_content: Option<String>,
        ...
    },

fn should_serialize_reasoning_content(content: &Option<Vec<ReasoningItemContent>>) -> bool {
    match content {
        Some(content) => !content
            .iter()
            .any(|c| matches!(c, ReasoningItemContent::ReasoningText { .. })),
        None => false,
    }
}
```

`skip_serializing_if` skips the field when the function returns `true`. The `Some` arm already follows that rule, since it skips content that carries no reasoning text. The `None` arm returns `false`, so an absent `content` gets written out as `null`. The function's name says the opposite of how serde uses it, which is probably how that arm ended up inverted.

**The schema has no null branch.** In [`openai/openai-openapi` `openapi.yaml` L61884-L61889](https://github.com/openai/openai-openapi/blob/571c56a2b4c2a8c099de1ab0945923e21e4265f2/openapi.yaml#L61884-L61889), `ReasoningItem.content` is:

```yaml
        content:
          type: array
          description: |
            Reasoning text content.
          items:
            $ref: "#/components/schemas/ReasoningTextContent"
```

`content` is not in the item's `required` list ([L61899-L61902](https://github.com/openai/openai-openapi/blob/571c56a2b4c2a8c099de1ab0945923e21e4265f2/openapi.yaml#L61899-L61902) lists `id`, `summary`, and `type`). A conformant request therefore either omits it or sends an array. The spec marks nullable fields where it means them: the sibling `encrypted_content` ([L61852-L61877](https://github.com/openai/openai-openapi/blob/571c56a2b4c2a8c099de1ab0945923e21e4265f2/openapi.yaml#L61852-L61877)) is explicitly `anyOf: [{type: string}, {type: "null"}]`, and `content` has no such branch. (This is also why #42368, about `encrypted_content: null`, is a separate question. That field is nullable in the spec.)

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

I ran a multi-turn, tool-using `codex exec` task with a loopback recording proxy between Codex and xAI's Responses endpoint. The task was to run `wc -l` on a file, run `git log --oneline -1`, and compute `17 + 25`. The provider entry used `wire_api = "responses"`, with `-c model_reasoning_effort=high`.

1. **Turn 1.** xAI returns a reasoning output item with the keys `encrypted_content`, `id`, `status`, `summary`, and `type`. It has **no `content` key**.
2. **Turn 2.** Codex replays that item and adds `content: null`. This is the captured request item, with the encrypted blob truncated:

   ```json
   {
     "type": "reasoning",
     "id": "rs_dcfdfd32-5ca4-954d-8d94-3edf6a41315b",
     "summary": [{"type": "summary_text", "text": "The user wants me to: ..."}],
     "content": null,
     "encrypted_content": "5ZpjTt4z5gZl90nr0ZJf...35vb"
   }
   ```

   I diffed this against the turn-1 item after removing xAI's `status` from one side and Codex's `content` from the other. The two are identical, and the 416-byte `encrypted_content` is replayed unmodified.
3. **Rejection.** xAI answers HTTP 400 and the turn fails:

   ```
   {"code":"invalid-argument","error":"Could not decode the compaction blob. Ensure it is unmodified from the compact response."}
   ```

   That message blames the blob, but the blob is untouched. If the proxy also strips `encrypted_content`, the same request gets a 422 that names the real field:

   ```
   input[3]: invalid "reasoning" item: content: invalid type: null, expected a sequence
   ```

4. **One-key control.** If the proxy deletes only the `content: null` key and changes nothing else, turn 2 returns 200. The task then completes with the correct results, and reasoning is replayed intact.

Turn-by-turn status codes for each proxy mode:

| Proxy mode | Status codes |
|---|---|
| pass-through | `200, 400` |
| strip `encrypted_content` | `200, 422 ×6` |
| drop reasoning items entirely | `200, 200` |
| **drop only `content: null`** | **`200, 200`** |

The same breakage was reported against OpenRouter in #11834, so it is not specific to xAI. It should affect any Responses endpoint that validates `input` against the schema.

### What is the expected behavior?

When `content` is `None`, the key should be omitted from the serialized reasoning item. That matches the schema, and it matches what the provider returned on turn 1.

### Additional information

**Suggested fix.** Invert the `None` arm:

```diff
 fn should_serialize_reasoning_content(content: &Option<Vec<ReasoningItemContent>>) -> bool {
     match content {
         Some(content) => !content
             .iter()
             .any(|c| matches!(c, ReasoningItemContent::ReasoningText { .. })),
-        None => false,
+        None => true,
     }
 }
```

It would also help to rename the function to `should_skip_reasoning_content` so the name matches how it is used, and to add a serializer test. The sketch below is untested:

```rust
let item = ResponseItem::Reasoning {
    id: None,
    summary: vec![],
    content: None,
    encrypted_content: Some("blob".to_string()),
    internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough: None,
};
let v = serde_json::to_value(&item).unwrap();
assert!(v.get("content").is_none(), "{v}");
```

Deserialization is unaffected, because `#[serde(default)]` still maps an absent key to `None`. For OpenAI's endpoint, omitting an optional field is just as valid as sending the null it currently tolerates.

**Why not the alternatives.**
- `"content": []` is schema-legal, but it claims the reasoning had text content, which the provider never returned.
- Leaving the fix to each provider means every schema-strict endpoint has to special-case a value the spec forbids.
- A per-provider compatibility flag adds configuration for a one-arm serializer bug.

**Not in scope here.** xAI's misleading "compaction blob" error message is theirs to fix. #42368 (`encrypted_content: null`) concerns a different field and gets a different answer from the spec.

items.body:
### Summary

The Chrome plugin in Codex Desktop on Windows is unusable in this environment. Chrome can be discovered as an extension-backed browser, but listing tabs or opening a requested page fails with `nodeRepl.fetch request failed`.

This is an additional environment report on a newer desktop package than #45249. Please link or consolidate it with the existing tracking issue if appropriate. The root cause has not been established.

### Environment

- OS: Windows 10 Pro, version 10.0.19045, build 19045, x64.
- Codex desktop MSIX package: `OpenAI.Codex_26.915.4065.0_x64` (verified from the running application path).
- Bundled Chrome / Computer Use component manifests: `26.915.31945`.
- Google Chrome installed binary version: `153.0.8010.53`.
- Chrome connection extension version: `1.26.901.11451_0`.
- Extension ID: `hehggadaopoacecdllhhajmbjkdcmajg`.
- Local HTTP proxy software is present. The environment's `NO_PROXY` contains `localhost,127.0.0.1,::1`. No controlled proxy A/B test was completed in this report.
- Observed repeatedly during troubleshooting on September 23–24, 2026.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open Chrome using a profile with the OpenAI connection extension installed and enabled.
2. Open a local Codex desktop task and invoke `@Chrome` with an ordinary navigation/search request.
3. The browser-control runtime can successfully execute `await cua.listBrowsers()` and return a Chrome backend with `family: "chrome"` and `type: "extension"`.
4. Use the exact returned browser ID to request its tabs, for example `await cua.listTabs({browser: "2"})` when the discovered ID is `2`.
5. The call fails with `nodeRepl.fetch request failed`. Earlier repetitions took approximately 21 seconds; the most recent repetition took approximately 14.6 seconds.
6. Opening a new Chrome tab through `cua.createBrowserTab("chrome", ...)` also failed. Its completion could not be verified because the subsequent tab-list call failed as well.

### Expected behavior

Codex should list the tabs in the discovered Chrome profile, open the requested page, and return readable page state.

### Actual behavior

```text
cua.listBrowsers(): Chrome extension backend discovered
cua.listTabs({browser: "<returned-id>"}): nodeRepl.fetch request failed
cua.createBrowserTab("chrome", ...): nodeRepl.fetch request failed
```

At other points the Chrome backend disappeared between discovery and selection, producing `Browser is not available`.

The latest failed attempt also emitted networking errors for requests to `ab.chatgpt.com` from the Statsig client. Those errors occurred alongside the browser-control failure; causation has not been established. Full request URLs and query parameters are intentionally omitted.

### Checks already completed

- The desktop settings UI reports Google Chrome as installed, with browsing allowed.
- Both `chrome@openai-bundled` and `computer-use@openai-bundled` have `enabled = true` in the local configuration.
- There was a difference between Chrome profiles: the default profile did not have the extension during the latest inventory, while another profile had it installed and enabled. Opening the enabled profile restored browser discovery, but tab listing still failed. This does not fully explain the problem.
- The bundled native-host-manifest diagnostic returned `correct: true`, with matching registry/manifest paths and the expected allowed extension origins.
- The native messaging host executable exists, and `extension-host.exe` was observed running during reproduction.
- Resetting the browser tool's JavaScript session did not restore control.
- Bringing the current Codex task to the foreground and reopening its browser panel temporarily restored some discovery responses, but Chrome tab operations continued to fail.
- Restarting the desktop app/browser and checking the extension were already tried by the user without resolution.

### Additional diagnostic clue

Desktop logs repeatedly include:

```text
No ChatGPT browser route is available for browser session <redacted-current-task-id>
```

Some consecutive in-app-browser `getInfo` requests failed and then succeeded; similar failures later recurred. This may be relevant to task/session routing, but it has not been proven to cause the Chrome failure.

### Impact and requested help

The issue has blocked ordinary browser work for the user over an extended period. Please investigate the Windows browser-control request path after successful backend discovery, and provide either a verified fix/workaround or a supported way to obtain the underlying transport error code.

### Related reports

- #45249 — Chrome discovery succeeds but listTabs fails after approximately 21 seconds.
- #47123 — Windows browser/session discovery still fails after IPC rebuild.
- #45028 — IAB route disappears after successful getInfo.
- #45340 — visible built-in browser cannot be enumerated.

Only the checks above were performed in this environment. Troubleshooting steps from the linked reports are not being claimed as performed here.

### Privacy

This report includes only selected diagnostic facts. It does not attach screenshots, raw logs, conversation contents, account identifiers, profile names, private local paths, tokens, cookies, or browser storage.

labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

items.body:
## What happened

When the account usage limit is reached mid-session, `codex app-server` emits, for every turn started afterwards, the notification sequence

```
account/rateLimits/updated
thread/status/changed
error
turn/completed
```

and the turn ends within about one second. Because the turn is reported as `turn/completed` (not `turn/failed`), a driver that keys success on `turn/completed` treats it as a normal completion and immediately starts the next turn. In our orchestrator this produced ~1,300 sub-second turns per hour for several hours until the account limit refilled, and the per-turn side effects (tracker API reads) exhausted a third-party rate limit as well.

## What I expected

A turn that ends because of an `error` notification (usage limit exhausted, or any other terminal error) should be reported as `turn/failed` with the error in `params`, or at minimum `turn/completed` should not follow an `error` for the same turn. Drivers should be able to rely on `turn/completed` meaning "the turn ran".

## Environment

- codex-cli 0.155.1 (standalone, `codex app-server`), Linux x86_64
- Driver: an Elixir orchestrator that launches one app-server turn per tracker issue over stdio and waits for `turn/completed` / `turn/failed`

## Notes

- The `error` notification payload was not captured by the driver at the time; the ordering above is from the driver's per-notification log.
- Workaround on the driver side: treat an in-turn `error` notification as a turn failure and back off.

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using?

`OpenAI.Codex 26.917.8451.0`

### What platform is your computer?

Windows x64. PowerShell 7.6.6.

### What issue are you seeing?

Codex Desktop launches multiple `ChatGPT.exe` background processes but never creates a visible window.

All observed `ChatGPT.exe` processes remained responsive, but every process had:

```text
Responding         True
MainWindowHandle   0
MainWindowTitle    <empty>
```

Example from the affected launch:

```text
Id    Responding MainWindowHandle MainWindowTitle
20000 True       0
25544 True       0
30824 True       0
37708 True       0
43900 True       0
51468 True       0
```

The failure correlates with `cua_node` runtime materialization never finalizing.

Under:

```text
%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\runtimes\cua_node
```

the previous finalized runtime existed:

```text
df473e5367fa2b42
```

but every launch of 26.917.8451.0 created a new staging directory for the new runtime ID:

```text
.staging-7f75cff94511d5f8-<random>
```

and never produced:

```text
7f75cff94511d5f8
```

Repeated launches accumulated many staging directories, including several created minutes apart on 2026-09-24.

Deleting all stale `.staging-*` directories did not fix the problem. On the next launch, Codex immediately created another `.staging-7f75cff94511d5f8-*` directory and again stayed headless.

### Reproduction / observed sequence

1. Install/update Codex Desktop to `26.917.8451.0` on Windows.
2. Launch Codex.
3. Several `ChatGPT.exe` processes start, but no window appears.
4. `Get-Process ChatGPT | Select Id,Responding,MainWindowHandle,MainWindowTitle` shows every process with `MainWindowHandle = 0`.
5. Inspect `%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\runtimes\cua_node`.
6. A new `.staging-7f75cff94511d5f8-<random>` directory appears, but the finalized `7f75cff94511d5f8` directory is never created.
7. Kill ChatGPT and the sandbox service, delete the staging directory, and launch again.
8. Another staging directory with the same runtime ID is created and the app remains headless.

### Confirmed workaround

I stopped all Codex-related processes:

```powershell
Get-Process ChatGPT -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Stop-Process -Force
Get-Process "codex-windows-sandbox-service" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Stop-Process -Force
```

Then I copied the complete packaged `cua_node` runtime into the expected finalized content-addressed directory using `xcopy /G`:

```powershell
$pkg = Get-AppxPackage OpenAI.Codex
$src = Join-Path $pkg.InstallLocation "app\resources\cua_node"
$dst = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\OpenAI\Codex\runtimes\cua_node\7f75cff94511d5f8"

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $dst | Out-Null
& "$env:SystemRoot\System32\xcopy.exe" "$src\*" "$dst\" /E /I /H /Y /G
```

Verification after copying:

```text
Runtime ID    : 7f75cff94511d5f8
node.exe      : True
node_repl.exe : True
manifest.json : True
file count    : 2283
```

After deleting the failed `.staging-*` directory and launching Codex again, **the window appeared immediately and the app worked normally**.

No changes were made to `~\.codex`, WindowsApps permissions, registry settings, or application binaries.

### Expected behavior

Codex should successfully materialize/finalize the bundled `cua_node` runtime and continue startup normally.

If runtime relocation fails, the app should show an actionable error instead of silently remaining headless with responsive background processes and `MainWindowHandle = 0`.

The runtime installer should also recover from incomplete staging state instead of creating a new failed `.staging-*` directory on every launch.

### Additional information

This appears to be a regression / continuation of the Windows runtime-relocation issue reported in #42412 and related earlier reports.

The important new data point is that the same failure still reproduces on **26.917.8451.0** with runtime ID **`7f75cff94511d5f8`**, and manually installing the complete packaged runtime with **`xcopy /G`** immediately restores the GUI.

### What issue are you seeing?

When using a custom `model_providers` entry pointing at a local vLLM server (`wire_api = "responses"`, plain HTTP over Tailscale, no proxy), Codex intermittently starts sending **truncated request bodies**: the server receives a JSON document cut off inside the first string value and correctly replies 400. From that point on, **every request issued by that Codex process fails within ~2 seconds with the same 400** — including brand-new turns. Only restarting the TUI process recovers it; a freshly started process works perfectly against the same server at the same time.

Server response received by Codex:

```json
{"error":{"message":"Unterminated string starting at: line 1 column 9 (char 8)","type":"BadRequestError","param":null,"code":400}}
```

- The request body arrives truncated within the first string value (~9 bytes in, e.g. cut right after `{"model":"`), so the server is parsing a genuinely partial body — yet the HTTP exchange itself completes and Codex receives the 400 cleanly.
- Once one request fails this way, all subsequent requests from the same process fail within ~2 s. 4 occurrences across 4 processes over 2 days of use; each process had to be restarted.
- The vLLM server log contains **no matching 4xx/5xx record** for the failing requests. Out-of-band server health checks were clean: 18 parallel probe requests all returned, and bodies up to ~800 KB arrive intact.

**Not sub-agent related.** Early occurrences coincided with multi-agent v2 subagent activity, but the bug reproduces with `[features] multi_agent = false` **and** `multi_agent_v2 = false` (2026-09-24: a plain session doing local `curl` + file reads, no subagent spawned at any point, hit the identical 400).

The common factor across all occurrences is a **long-lived TUI process** (hours of uptime). Worst case: the process had been running ~17 h including an overnight idle, and the first model request of the morning hit it.

This strongly suggests client-side request-serialization / connection-pool state corruption — e.g. a request buffer or chunked-framing state damaged after an aborted/completed SSE stream or a stale idle connection, then reused for subsequent requests.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Not deterministic yet. Best recipe so far:

1. Configure a custom provider with `wire_api = "responses"` against vLLM (plain HTTP, no proxy).
2. Keep a TUI session running for a long time (observed after ~17 h including an overnight idle; earlier occurrences after minutes-to-hours of active use).
3. Send a request → it fails with the 400 above; from then on every request in that process fails within ~2 s.

Failing thread id (2026-09-24 occurrence): `01a0cd9b-74a4-7a60-bad7-7004fb61eb8f` — two turn attempts recorded as `Turn error` with the identical 400 payload.

Frequency: 4 occurrences across 4 processes over 2 days of use.

### What is the expected behavior?

- Request bodies must always be complete, valid JSON regardless of prior stream aborts or stale idle connections.
- A failed/corrupt pooled connection should be discarded and retried on a fresh connection, not poison the pool for the lifetime of the process.

### Additional information

- Workaround: restarting the TUI recovers immediately — the only fix that works. Disabling sub-agents (`[features] multi_agent = false`, `multi_agent_v2 = false`) does **not** prevent it (disproved by the 2026-09-24 reproduction).
- Possibly related: #31376 (Responses HTTP requests can stall before response headers without a bounded retry — same transport area, different symptom).
- Questions:
  - Is there a supported way to disable HTTP keep-alive / force per-request connections for a custom provider?
  - Is there a flag to log raw request bodies client-side (e.g. `RUST_LOG=reqwest=trace`?) so the truncation can be captured at send time?

## Impact
Recurring desktop UI reinitialization interrupts active work on Windows. Please prioritize investigation and advise a supported recovery procedure or fixed build.

## Environment
- Codex desktop on Windows.
- Installed package path in the diagnostic log identifies version `26.917.8451.0` (not independently confirmed by package inventory).
- Renderer telemetry: build `10789`, commit `eaa425e88319d39061158ee2b5eb141ad7a9dd19`.
- Time zone: Asia/Bangkok (UTC+07:00).

## Observed behavior
The user reports that the app closes and reopens itself while using an existing task. The latest logs show repeated renderer initialization and internal RPC disconnections; they do not establish that the whole desktop process crashes every time. During inspection, the task API continued to report an active turn without a turn error. Whether the task was progressing normally was not established.

## Latest incident: 24 September 2026
- At **02:13:50.975 UTC / 09:13:50.975 local**, `Renderer-local AppServerManager RPC disconnected` with `errorMessage="no such export ID: 114"`.
- Subsequently repeated `Peer closed MessagePort connection.`, with heartbeat hydration, pinned-thread synchronization, and invalid-message errors.
- **21** renderer-local AppServerManager RPC disconnections in the inspected log between **02:13:50.975 and 02:15:10.340 UTC**.
- Repeated `[startup][renderer] app routes mounted` events approximately every 3–5 seconds.
- At **02:15:10.419 UTC**, another task also logged `Failed to resume conversation` with `Peer closed MessagePort connection.`.
- A bounded Windows Application Event Log query for IDs 1000, 1001 and 1002 over the preceding two hours returned no matching Codex/ChatGPT entries. This does not rule out a crash.

## Earlier incident
Around **01:35 local on 24 September / 18:35 UTC on 23 September**: `Peer closed MessagePort connection.`, `write EPIPE`, and `MessagePort message error.`, followed by app-server transport stop. A new desktop log run began at 01:35:16 local. Its relationship to the latest renderer loop is unknown.

## Reproduction and expected behavior
Observed during normal use of an existing task; the exact triggering action and a reliable minimal reproduction are not established. The UI should remain usable, or recover its internal connection without repeated reinitialization or losing access to the task.

Root cause is unknown. These logs do not prove token exhaustion, insufficient memory, GPU failure, or a problem in the user's project. RPC errors may be consequences rather than the initiating fault.

No cache was deleted, no application binaries were modified, and no software was installed during diagnosis. This report includes selected diagnostic facts only, without raw session data, source code, account identifiers, credentials or local user paths.

Potentially related symptom report: #47291 also mentions `no such export ID`, but on macOS. A shared root cause has **not** been established.

Please investigate the renderer/AppServerManager RPC lifecycle and provide a recovery procedure that preserves task history and local work. Is there a build containing a fix?

    Important constraints in this project:
    - Do not add work to the render/main loop unless absolutely necessary.
    - Do not use broad polling or generic fallback logic when the real bug is local.
    - Prefer minimal, localized C++ changes.

Unwrap `AstraSelectedFromModelPicker` before dispatching its model update, then trigger the sparkle afterward when eligible. Keep the eligibility check and model update in the same event so queued backend updates cannot turn a no-op confirmation into a sparkle.

## Summary
For more than a week, the Windows Codex desktop app has been largely unusable for follow-up messages. A new conversation may accept its first message, but after the assistant finishes, typing another message leaves Send disabled/gray. Existing completed conversations behave similarly. The same conversation can still be continued from the Codex CLI. The issue persists after updating the desktop package to 26.917.8451.0.

## Environment
- Windows 11 Pro x64, OS build 26300
- Codex desktop package: 26.917.8451.0 (previously reproduced on 26.917.6896.0)
- Standalone Codex CLI: 0.156.1
- Desktop-bundled app-server binary reports: codex-cli 0.155.0-alpha.16.3

## Steps to reproduce
1. Open Codex desktop on Windows and open a completed conversation, or create a conversation and send its first message.
2. Wait for the assistant response to finish.
3. Type a follow-up message.
4. Observe that Send is disabled/gray and cannot be clicked.

**Expected:** The completed conversation accepts follow-up messages.

**Actual:** The desktop composer cannot send. Continuing the same conversation through the CLI works. Opening Settings and returning did not restore Send.

## Timeline and sanitized diagnostics
- **2026-09-23 morning (local time), package 26.917.6896.0:** A failing desktop session logged 22 `configRequirements/read` requests with no transport error, but no `turn-start config resolved` or `method=turn/start`.
- **2026-09-23 17:51 (local), same package 26.917.6896.0:** A new desktop session temporarily worked without updating the app. It logged 21 `configRequirements/read` requests, then 3 `turn-start config resolved` and 3 `method=turn/start` events.
- **2026-09-24 at ~09:04 and ~09:15 (local):** The failure returned. The 09:04 session logged 13 `configRequirements/read` requests with no transport error and no turn-start event.
- **2026-09-24 09:44:57 (local), after updating to 26.917.8451.0:** The new desktop process still failed. The session again had roughly 13 `configRequirements/read` events with `errorCode=null`, but no `turn-start config resolved` or `method=turn/start`. For example:
  ```text
  2026-09-24T01:45:08.012Z response_routed method=configRequirements/read errorCode=null hadPending=true durationMs=9
  2026-09-24T01:45:08.024Z response_routed method=windowsSandbox/readiness errorCode=null hadPending=true durationMs=19
  ```

These lines show that the app's main-process routing received RPC responses without a transport error. They do not establish whether the renderer consumed them, nor do they establish the sandbox readiness result. The exact root cause is unconfirmed. The contrast with the working session may help locate why the desktop client does not proceed to `turn/start`.

An in-app feedback report was also submitted: `no-active-thread-01a0d11d-8ed8-71b3-8e2e-3db9f1a33241`.

Possibly related reports: #45626, #46584.

## Additional client comparison (2026-09-24)
The Chrome browser extension side panel can send messages, including a follow-up in this conversation, while the Windows desktop app has the disabled Send button. Together with the working CLI, this points toward a desktop-client-specific path. The comparison does not identify the exact failing component; the extension and desktop may use different client code or connection paths.

Appending output to the completion transcript and pending polling buffer under separate locks allows cancellation to interrupt a chunk update between the two buffers.

items.title: Goals can repeat the same assistant response hundreds of times after automatic context compaction

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: model-behavior
